description.narrative: AECF-Renewable Energy and Climate Change Adaptation (REACT) is a challenge fund that aims to co-finance and stimulate, innovative private investments in renewable energy and climate adaptation in Tanzania. It is implemented by AGRA (Alliance for Green Revloution in Africa).

Det tredje rundan av AECF REACT kommer att utlysas som en tävling där företag ansöker om finansiering för innovativa affärsidéer inom förnybar energi. Syftet är att öka tillgången till förnybar energi till låg kostnad samt anpassning till klimatförändringar på den tanzaniska landsbygden genom ökade affärsinvesteringar och nya affärsmodeller.
Det övergripande syftet med insatsen är att bidra till minskad fattigdom i Tanzania genom förbättrad tillgång till energi och minskad sårbarhet i förhållande till klimatförändringar. Insatsen ska främja företags investeringar och innovationer inom billig förnybar energi och klimatanpassningsteknologi genom att erbjuda lån och bidrag som företagen måste matcha med minst motsvarande summa. Ansökningar måste visa tydlig fattigdomsinriktning tex genom att bidra till ökade inkomster, jobbskapande och produktivitet eller minsakde kostander för fattiga människor.

The overall goal of REACT is to contribute to reducing rural poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa. The purpose is to catalyse private sector investment and innovation in low cost clean energy and adaptation to climate change technologies. The overall driving forces are that the business idea must show an environmental benefit and that it must demonstrate a positive impact on the rural poor through increased incomes, employment and productivity or reduced costs.
Renewable Energy and Adaptation to Climate Technologies (REACT) is a climate change window of the Africa Enterprise Challenge Fund (AECF). REACT uses the AECF challenge fund approach with the aim of incentivizing private sector delivery of low cost clean energy and climate adaptation technologies to help rural beneficiaries adjust to climate change and escape poverty. AECF uses grant funding to catalyze greater investment into these sectors, sharing risks that these businesses face. These results taken from REACT Project Closeout Report which covers the period of October 2010 to 30th June 2023 which provides a summary of the performance against the work plan of AECF Renewable Energy and Adaptation to Climate Technologies (REACT) for round 1 to 3, Impact , key challenges and lessons learned, as observed in sections below. The Embassy assesses that the overall, REACT has successfully incentivized the private sector to sustain innovative new products and services, with notable achievement in the solar home system sector
Competitions: During the implementation period of the contribution, a total of three competitions were launched and supported 19 projects with different technologies, and business models (for all rounds R1, R2 and R3). The use of competitive challenge funds was meant to allow investees to design innovative business models for promoting and increasing access to renewable energy and climate technologies.
Funds disbursement to Investees: REACT R1&R2, a total of USD 6,699,451 (grant USD 3,419,635 and loan USD 3,279,816) was committed to 10 Projects with a disbursement of USD 6,113,183 (grant USD 2,945,149 and loan USD 3,168,184), representing 91% of utilization.
REACT R3, a total of USD 6,671,333 (grant USD 2,625,894 and loan USD 4,045,439) was committed to 9 projects with disbursement of USD 5,324,415 (grant USD 2,408,394 and loan USD 2,916,021), representing 80% utilization.
Undisbursed funds: At the closure, there was an actual balance of USD 1,116,680 that was allocated to Jumeme Hydro Power but was not drawn down due to delays in signing the Standardized Power Purchase Agreement (SPPA) with the off taker (TANESCO) and failure to obtain the matching funds despite extending their contract to June 2023.
Investees performance snapshot: Rounds 1 and 2 Among the companies supported, Mobisol GmbH and Off Grid Electric, promoting solar home systems, demonstrated commendable performance. Mobisol successfully reached over 134,000 households, while Off Grid Electric extended its services to 170,000 households. The core of their business model involved the sale of solar home systems bundled with appliances, providing households access to credit with a repayment period spanning 3 to 4 years. Notably, some of the appliances facilitated income generating activities, empowering beneficiaries to generate revenue and manage their loan obligations effectively.
However, the performance of Husk Power Systems, Sandali Wood Industries, and SimGas projects fell short of expectations. Husk Power System and SimGas encountered challenges with their business model and technology, while Sandali Wood Industries faced hurdles due to bureaucratic obstacles in obtaining necessary permits, licenses, and uncertainties related to forestry policies.
Additionally, four projects EGG Energy, Kiwia & Laustsen, East Africa Power, and Field Masters were prematurely closed due to the inability to secure the required matching funds and issues related to technology or business model failures.
Round 3 Despite the challenges posed by the COVID19 pandemic, two adaptation projects, namely East Africa Fruits Farm and Co. Ltd, and Net Health Ltd, demonstrated strong performance both in business and development impacts. East Africa Fruits Farm provided extension services to smallholder farmers cultivating vegetables and fruits, ultimately purchasing their produce at a premium compared to middlemen. The project exceeded its target, benefiting households by 20%. Net Health Ltd, specializing in the production of affordable agronets as an alternative to traditional greenhouse materials, enabled horticulture farmers to manage pests and diseases, cultivate high value crops, and produce premium quality goods. Although faced with entry barriers, including farmer reluctance to adopt new technology, Net Health reached over 1,500 smallholder farmers (approximately 40% of the target) through effective distribution networks and a robust marketing strategy.
In contrast, two minigrid projects, Jumeme Rural Power Supply and Suma Hydro Ltd, experienced significant delays attributed to various factors, including challenges with technology and business models, insufficient matching funds, policy unpredictability, and uncertainties related to grid extension. The regulatory landscape concerning the Standardized Power Purchase Agreement (SPPA) posed persistent challenges, leading to slow implementation and frozen activities. Discussions and negotiations with TANESCO on the power purchase agreement faced prolonged delays since 2017, preventing the utilization of allocated funds. However, Luponde Hydro Ltd, another minigrid project, overcame obstacles after several years, successfully developing a 0.9 MW site commissioned in June 2019. The second site's development (2 MW) was delayed due to the signing delay of the SPPA necessary to unlock funds.
Dobea Group Ltd, focusing on microgrid development, encountered difficulties in raising matching funds and uncertainties related to grid extension. In response to grid extension uncertainties, the investee contemplated relocating to islands to safeguard their investments, resulting in the inability to draw down allocated funds.
Closed projects before the end of the programme: Five contracted projects were closed early due to several reasons including business model failure, inadequate or lack of matching funds and noncompliance.
Loan disbursed, repayments and write offs: A total USD 6,084,055 was disbursed to 11 investees as loans, with USD 662,000 going to one investee under R1, USD 2,506,034 distributed to three investees under R2, and USD 2,916,021 provided to seven investees under R3. Out of the disbursed loan amount, a total of USD 2,940,734 was repaid by six investees, including USD 1,291,688 from two companies in R2 and USD 1,649,046 from four companies in R3. Notably, Powergen, an investee in R3, is actively servicing its outstanding loan of USD 158,642, with an expectation to clear the balance by the end of 2023.
Furthermore, loans amounting to USD 2,984,679 were written off from six investees, encompassing USD 662,000 from R1, USD 1,214,346 from R2, and USD 1,108,333 from R3, as detailed in the provided table 6 in the attached report. The justification for these write offs was based on business model or technology failures leading to insufficient cash flow to service the loans.
Key results and achievements: REACT Tanzania engaged a total of 19 companies through three competitions. A total of USD 11,437,598 of investment capital was disbursed inform of non repayable grants and repayable grants of USD 5,353,543 and USD 6,084,055 respectively. Nearly half of the disbursed repayable grants, specifically USD 2,940,734, were successfully repaid. The companies secured additional funds amounting to more than USD 39.2 million as matching contributions, thereby resulting in a threefold leverage of the funding from REACT Tanzania.
REACT Tanzania impacted 743,303 individuals through access and adoption of renewable energy technologies and services, translating to an installed off-grid electricity capacity of 3.8MW, and resulting in annual emission reductions of 107,630 tCO2eq. A total of 591 jobs were created through this programme.
Key Insights and Lessons Learned: - Most supported companies were startups at an early stage of commercialization. This posed some challenges such as delayed matching funds and legal and regulatory navigation. The AECF patient capital assisted these companies to unlock funds from other sources. Access to patient capital with flexible conditions is important to early stage businesses.
- Predictable government policies and plans are important in renewable energy investments. Mini grids investments were hardly hit by unpredictable policies and plans in the country in particular standardized power purchase agreement (SPPA). Favorable grid extension and rural electrification government plans, policies and regulations should be in place to facilitate private sector players to invest, particularly for mini grids.
- The investee ability to promptly respond to unexpected external shocks and circumstances is crucial for business survival. Investees who responded to COVID19 pandemic by adjusting their plans, strategies and models were not affected significantly.
- Testing of the new business model/technology and growing them organically is important for businesses sustainability. Investees need to test the new technology or business model and grow gradually depending on the market response.
- Upfront financing is crucial to investments in rural areas. Rural communities in Tanzania generally have lower incomes but are willing to pay for modern energy service if appropriate consumer financing is in place. Rural households require solar energy solutions beyond basic electricity services i.e. lighting and phone charging. Customers need systems that can power home appliances such as stereo, hair clippers, iron, televisions sets and refrigerator e.t.c, for both households and productive use.
- Businesses that sell products to customers on credit need to structure flexible repayment plans that accommodate customers seasonal cash flow. Most rural households rely on agriculture as their main economic activity therefore their income is not stable throughout the year rather it fluctuates with peak during harvesting seasons.
- Development partners supporting promotion of renewable energy technologies should have flexibility during implementation of renewable energy initiatives. This is to accommodate changing circumstances during implementation of such initiatives for instance extending programme duration to accommodate the challenges faced by Investees while raising matching funds.
